title: How To Give Your Students Unforgettable Directions
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin distinguishes between simple, immediate directions — best given directly and unambiguously — and lengthy, multi-step directions, which he argues require a storytelling approach to stick. He offers seven techniques for the latter: framing directions as a narrative, using the phrase 'going to' to prompt visualization, embedding small silly 'anchor' tasks along the way, acting out the steps physically, sketching a visual winding path of tasks on the board, placing responsibility on students by asking if anyone is unsure before starting, and gradually increasing the complexity of the challenge as students improve. He closes by warning that failing to teach directions this way creates needy, dependent students who default to seeking help rather than working independently.
points: Simple, immediate directions should be given directly and unambiguously, while lengthy multi-step directions require a storytelling approach to be remembered.
Using the phrase 'going to' throughout directions is described as a memory device that prompts students to visualize themselves completing each step.
Embedding small, silly 'anchor' tasks (like touching a basketball pole) along a set of directions helps students remember the full sequence.
A visual winding path of boxes, sketched on the board with one- or two-word reminders per box, reinforces the story structure of an activity.
Asking 'Is there anyone who doesn't know exactly what to do' before releasing students places responsibility for understanding directly on them.
quotes: Your students will pay close attention if you make your directions sound like a story progressing from beginning to end.

Going to” is a memory device that causes students to create a moving picture in their mind. It’s also predictive. They take it as fact that they’ll indeed be able to do everything you ask them—without your help.

Silly tasks like this act as anchors along a memory map for your students. The novelty and goofiness has a way of helping them remember the path that leads from the beginning of the activity to the successful end.
By being proactive and asking if anyone doesn’t understand, you effectively put the onus of speaking up on your students—saddling them with a greater feeling of responsibility to do it right.

Many teachers place giving individual help at the top of their priority list and don’t give a second thought to how they provide the directions—which creates needy, dependent students whose first inclination is to look to their teacher rather than relying on themselves.
